question_text: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He has a 3-month history of a nonproductive cough. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Physical examination and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

                    ### Question
                    A 34-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He has a 3-month history of a nonproductive cough. He is 177 cm (5 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 100 kg (220.46 lbs); BMI is 35.1 kg/m2. His temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Physical examination and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with a persistent nonproductive cough despite treatment with diphenhydramine, and chest x-ray shows no abnormalities. Given the lack of response to antihistamines, the cough may be due to non-allergic rhinitis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), or asthma. Pulmonary function testing is appropriate to assess for asthma, which is a common cause of chronic cough and can be exacerbated by obesity. Omeprazole may be considered if GERD is suspected, but without further evidence of reflux symptoms, it is less immediately warranted. A CT scan could provide more detail but is not the first-line approach without further indication. Oral corticosteroids are typically reserved for confirmed asthma or inflammatory conditions. Azithromycin is not indicated as the symptoms do not suggest a bacterial infection. Therefore, the most appropriate next step in management is pulmonary function testing to evaluate for asthma.
